title: Plans from the Pawn Centre
subtitle: Attack the king or challenge the centre

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter VI, §31 Some Salient Points About Pawns, Example 64

narration.say: This is a pawn-structure diagram, not a complete game. The original omits both kings. Kings on h1 and h8 are technical placeholders for the app.
White has pawns on d4 and e5. Black has pawns on d5 and e6. This structure commonly arises in the French Defence.
The advanced pawn on e5 gains space and controls d6 and f6.
Capablanca describes White’s central pawns as attacking, and Black’s as defensive. These descriptions concern plans, not a forced result.
In a complete position with developed pieces, White often prepares f4 and f5 to attack the kingside.
These arrows show a plan, not a supplied move sequence. No moves are played in this diagram lesson.
Black’s counterplay is the pawn break c5, attacking the base of White’s centre on d4.
White may support d4 with c3. Black then concentrates pieces against the centre instead of passively defending the king.

steps.title: Pawn advances commit you to a structure

narration.say: Advancing a central pawn changes the squares it controls and the lines available to the pieces. Consider the resulting structure before making the advance.
Capablanca also discusses passed pawns: their power depends on support, blockade, and how many pieces remain. Being passed is not by itself a guarantee of strength.

steps.title: Connect the wings to the centre

narration.say: White’s kingside attack and Black’s central counterplay are connected. Weakening the centre can undermine the attack.
Study the pawn skeleton first, then decide where the pieces belong. The placeholder kings are not part of the original diagram.
